state.misconception_label: Does not understand a percentage is out of 100

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Convert this percentage to a fraction \( 62 \% \). I got \( \frac{62}{10} \) because I treated the percent as if it were already a fraction over 1.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about if you were dividing a pizza into slices. If you have 62% of a pizza, how many out of 100 slices would that be?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you mean about the pizza. So if I have 62% of a pizza, that would be like having 62 out of 100 slices? But why do we always think of percentages as being out of 100? Isn’t it just a way to show part of something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about it like this: if you have 62 out of 100 slices of pizza, that means you have 62% of the whole pizza. Percentages are always out of 100 because it helps us compare different amounts easily. Imagine you were dividing up a big box of candy into 100 smaller packages — each percentage tells you how many of those packages you would have.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the specific misconception that percentages aren't necessarily out of 100 using concrete analogies, the student demonstrates clear progress in understanding (moving from 62/10 to recognizing 62/100), though the cognitive demand relies more on guided analogy than independent reasoning.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (pizza slices, candy packages) to explain the abstract concept that percentages represent parts out of 100, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
